w: What's tested Ginglymoarthrodial joint; "one bone, two joints"; rotation in the lower compartment, translation in the upper The disc (intermediate zone, borders, medial thickness, not a meniscus) and the retrodiscal tissues Ligaments and what each one limits (capsular, discal, stylomandibular, sphenomandibular, TM inner and outer) Each muscle of mastication: roughly where it attaches, its form and its job; the two bellies of the masseter and of the lateral pterygoid The exam slide of muscles for each mandibular movement (Dr. Givan: the answer "will come from this slide") Suprahyoid vs infrahyoid groups and the floating hyoid This lecture looks at anatomy "from a clinician's point of view": less about every fossa and ridge, more about how the parts work. Dr. Givan said he presented it at the level he would test; he does not plan to ask about innervation or blood supply, which you covered in gross anatomy. A complex joint Dogs and alligators hinge and tear; cows and camels grind with large side-to-side motion; we are in between. A ginglymus joint moves in one plane like a hinge (elbow, knee, finger joints). An arthrodial joint glides between flat surfaces (wrist, ankle, spine). The TMJ does both: a ginglymoarthrodial joint. And it is one bone with two joints: no movement of one side happens without the other, so neither TMJ moves independently. Opening starts as pure rotation about the transverse horizontal axis, then adds translation. The articular disc The disc is dense fibrous connective tissue that functions like a bone, which makes the TMJ a compound joint. From the side it is biconcave: a thick anterior border, a thinner intermediate zone, and an even thicker posterior border. The condyle normally sits in the intermediate zone, which is completely avascular with no nerves. From the front, the disc is slightly thicker medially than laterally, so if it slips off the condyle it tends to go forward or medially. The heights of contour of the condyle are the medial and lateral poles. It is improper to call the disc a meniscus, which is crescent-shaped (convex and concave sides), as in the knee. The disc is attached front and back, dividing the joint into an upper (superior) compartment, disc to temporal bone, where translation happens, and a lower (inferior) compartment, disc to condyle, where rotation happens. So the disc stays over the condyle wherever it goes, always there to cushion. Behind it are the retrodiscal tissues, loaded with vessels and nerves; functioning on them causes substantial pain. Of the two retrodiscal laminae, the superior is elastic and the inferior is collagenous. In front, the superior head of the lateral pterygoid attaches to the capsule and disc and the inferior head to the condylar neck. The articulating surfaces are covered by resilient, collagenous, fluid-filled tissue; they are not meant to touch each other, and when a perforated disc lets bone meet bone, the joint breaks down. The joint is load-bearing. To crush a bolus you need something to pivot against, and that is the seated joint, which is why the condyles seat essentially every time the elevator muscles contract. The condyle's trabecular structure is built like a bridge to carry that force. Ligaments limit motion Capsular Condylar neck to the articular eminence and fossa, wrapping the joint like a curtain Encases the joint; resists downward displacement Medial and lateral discal (collateral) Disc to the medial and lateral poles of the condyle Keep the disc on the condyle; stretched or torn = clicking (about half of a class clicks) Stylomandibular Styloid process to the angle and posterior border of the ramus Limits opening and forward motion Sphenomandibular Spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandibular foramen Limits opening and forward motion TM ligament, outer oblique portion Sling around the posterior condylar neck to the articular eminence Limits rotational opening TM ligament, inner horizontal portion Articular eminence to the disc and condylar head Limits posterior movement of the condyle and disc (protects against a blow to the chin) Ligaments don't heal, so stretched discal ligaments require other adaptations. If a patient can't close after a long appointment, the condyle may be stuck in front of the eminence (an open lock). Apply gentle downward pressure on the buccal shelf to distract it, "not a posterior force." How muscles work Muscles only pull, like a rope. They work as agonist-antagonist pairs, and the opposing muscle never fully turns off, which gives smooth movement at the right speed and force. Muscle fibers are grouped into units that can be activated separately, so one muscle can produce several movements (e.g. the temporalis elevates, protrudes or retrudes). Design depends on the surface available for attachment, speed of contraction, range of movement and force of contraction. Look at a muscle's shape and orientation and you can predict what it does. The muscles of mastication (supramandibular) Masseter Flat, thick, quadrangular; most superficial Zygomatic arch and malar process → angle of the ramus (and coronoid process) Power closer. Superficial belly: elevation + some protrusion. Deep belly: elevation + retrusion. About 50° between the bellies Temporalis Flat, fan-shaped, bipennate Temporal fossa and fascia → coronoid process Positioner, not a power closer. Anterior: elevation; middle: elevation + some retrusion; posterior: retrusion + some elevation Lateral pterygoid Triangular, two heads Superior head: infralateral greater wing of the sphenoid and infratemporal crest → capsule and disc. Inferior head: lateral surface of the lateral pterygoid plate → pterygoid fovea of the condylar neck Inferior head: opening and protrusion; one side alone = movement to the opposite side. Superior head: active in closure, stabilizing the disc Medial pterygoid Rhomboidal Medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate (plus palatine process and maxillary tuberosity) → inferoposterior medial surface of the ramus Elevation; with the masseter forms the pterygomasseteric sling The masseter is not vertical: its fibers run up and forward, so contracting it pushes the mandible superiorly and anteriorly, which is exactly the seated (CR) position. When the jaw is wide open the big superficial belly is folded back without mechanical advantage, so the deep belly starts the closure and swings the superficial belly into position to crush. The temporalis inserts on the thin coronoid process: "your first thought should be, that's not a power position." It is the jaw's major, fast positioner, aligning the teeth for chewing and shaping the cavity for speech, and its posterior fibers pull the mandible back. It is so important that the zygomatic arch forms a tunnel to protect its insertion. The lateral pterygoid is really two muscles ("could I just rename these muscles?"). The inferior head pulls the condyle forward, down and toward the midline: both sides = protrusion and opening; one side = the chin swings to the other side ("if I contract on the right side, I will move my jaw to the left"). The superior head is relaxed during opening and active during closure, balancing the elastic pull of the superior retrodiscal lamina so the disc returns smoothly, and keeping the disc in place when you pivot on a bolus. The medial pterygoid is "the unsung hero": a meaty elevator on the inside of the ramus that, with the masseter outside, forms the powerful pterygomasseteric sling. The exam slide: muscles for each movement "If I ask a question regarding what muscle is involved in what motion, it will come from this slide," even though other sources list more contributors. And know which belly: "this slide does not signify which belly of the lateral pterygoid, I expect you to know this as well." Elevation Temporalis, medial pterygoid, masseter Depression Lateral pterygoid (inferior head) + suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscles Protrusion Lateral pterygoid (inferior head) + superficial masseter Retrusion Temporalis (horizontal, posterior fibers) + deep masseter Lateral to the right Right temporalis + right masseter; left lateral pterygoid + left medial pterygoid Lateral to the left Left temporalis + left masseter; right lateral pterygoid + right medial pterygoid Opening: the inframandibular muscles and the hyoid The antagonists of the closers lie below the mandible, divided by the hyoid bone, "one of the coolest bones in the body": it articulates with nothing and floats, and every horn and fossa is a muscle attachment. The suprahyoid (inframandibular) muscles, digastric, geniohyoid, mylohyoid and stylohyoid, help open the jaw. The infrahyoid muscles, sternohyoid, omohyoid, sternothyroid and thyrohyoid, stabilize the hyoid. To open, the infrahyoids first fix the hyoid "like a rock," then the suprahyoids pull the mandible down. The digastric has anterior and posterior bellies joined by an intermediate tendon on the hyoid and is a key opener; the mylohyoid forms the floor of the mouth; the geniohyoid matters for the tongue. To swallow, the teeth come together to stabilize the mandible and the hyoid is pulled forward to open the esophageal path. The superficial neck muscles (sternocleidomastoid and trapezius) act as a sling that maintains head position. Take-homes: the orientation, size and shape of a muscle tell you what it does, and the bones show how much force the system handles.
